summary: A Best Current Practice describing how to combine Mobile IPv4 with IKEv2 mobility and multihoming (MOBIKE) so enterprise users get both mobility and secure connectivity. The user stays protected when connecting from untrusted networks and keeps working when the device moves and picks up a new IP address, inside or outside the enterprise network.

plainLanguage.summary: When you move from one Wi-Fi network to another, your secret tunnel to work would usually break. This describes a way to keep the tunnel alive as your address changes, so your work connection carries on.

questions: how to keep vpn alive when ip address changes
how does mobile ipv4 work with ipsec vpn
what is a vpn tunnel inner address
subtitle: How a laptop keeps both its VPN tunnel and its Mobile IP session alive as it roams between trusted and untrusted networks.

tldr.problem: Enterprise users need secure access from untrusted networks and seamless mobility when their IP address changes, but earlier designs stacked two layers of Mobile IPv4 with a very high per-packet overhead.
tldr.mechanism: Inside the enterprise the mobile node uses plain Mobile IPv4. Outside, it builds an IKEv2 VPN tunnel, registers the tunnel inner address as its co-located care-of address, and uses MOBIKE to tell the VPN gateway when its address changes.
tldr.outcome: One Mobile IP tunnel runs inside one IPsec tunnel, with no external home agent. It applies only to IKEv2 VPN gateways and is a Best Current Practice.

today: RFC 5266 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 136) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 5265, published the same month.

sections.title: The Enterprise Roaming Problem
sections.content:
A typical enterprise network has a trusted intranet and an untrusted network (the Internet), separated by a demilitarized zone (DMZ) where a firewall and a VPN gateway sit. Users on untrusted networks usually set up an IPsec VPN tunnel to reach the intranet. On the trusted network no VPN is used, but users benefit from Mobile IPv4 when they move between subnets.

Earlier work (RFC 5265 and RFC 4093) combined Mobile IPv4 and IPsec VPNs without changing the VPN gateways, which meant two layers of Mobile IPv4: one home agent inside the intranet and one in the Internet or the DMZ. The RFC says the per-packet overhead is very high and that running two instances of Mobile IPv4 at once on a mobile node is challenging.

This document offers an alternative that needs only one layer. It works only when IKEv2 IPsec VPNs are used; IKEv1 gateways are not addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Working from the office and working from a cafe need different kinds of protection. The old way of switching between them was clumsy, and this memo gives a simpler way.

sections.title: The Solution in Brief
sections.content:
The mobile node has one home address that stays the same inside or outside the enterprise. Inside, it uses Mobile IP for movement between subnets. Outside, it sets up a VPN tunnel to the VPN gateway and keeps a valid binding at the internal home agent (i-HA).

The key trick is that the mobile node uses the VPN tunnel inner address (VPN-TIA), handed out by the gateway during IKE negotiation, as its co-located care-of address when registering with the i-HA. If the TIA changes, or the node attaches to another VPN gateway, it sends a new Registration Request using the new address.

If the node moves while outside and only its access network changes, it uses MOBIKE to tell the VPN gateway its new address. The i-HA does not notice as long as the node stays on the same gateway and the TIA is unchanged.

The result is a Mobile IP tunnel inside an IPsec tunnel. The mobile node MUST reverse tunnel through the home agent (RFC 3024) in this case.
sections.plainLanguage: Your laptop borrows an address from the work gateway and tells your home base about it. When you move, it only has to tell the gateway your new spot, and your home base never notices.

sections.title: The Three Access Modes
sections.content:
The document names three ways the mobile node can be attached, following RFC 5265:

  • f: Mobile IPv4 with a foreign agent care-of address, on a trusted network where a foreign agent is detected.
  • c: Mobile IPv4 with a co-located care-of address assigned by the access network, used after the node detects a trusted network.
  • mc: Mobile IPv4 over a MOBIKE-enabled IPsec VPN, with the VPN-TIA as the co-located care-of address. It is used only on an untrusted network, where a tunnel is needed to reach the trusted network.

By default the node configures an address on the access link with DHCP. It then tests whether the network is trusted by sending a Registration Request to the i-HA in co-located mode. It MUST NOT use a foreign agent care-of address with the i-HA on an untrusted network.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three ways to connect: at the office using a helper, at the office on your own, or from outside through a secret tunnel. Each has its own rules.

sections.title: Detecting Trusted Networks and Moving
sections.content:
Security boundary detection depends on whether the i-HA can be reached. When the node notices a change in connectivity, it sends a Registration Request to the i-HA without VPN encapsulation. If it receives a Registration Reply carrying the Trusted Networks Configured (TNC) extension, and the reply is integrity protected with the mobile node and home agent security association, it concludes it is on a trusted network. The retransmission count and timeout are configurable.

If the node already has a VPN tunnel, it MUST send a MOBIKE message at the same time as the registration request whenever its address changes. A reply from the VPN gateway but not from the i-HA means it is outside the enterprise; a reply from the i-HA means it is inside.

When moving from an untrusted network, the node starts an IKE mobility exchange and a plain registration at once. If the registration is answered, the subnet is trusted and the node MAY tear down the VPN. When moving from a trusted network, it does the same, and if no reply arrives but the VPN comes up, it registers over the tunnel with the i-HA and then communicates over the VPN using its home address.
sections.plainLanguage: Your laptop knocks on the office door without the tunnel. If someone answers, it knows it is at work and can drop the tunnel. If not, it uses the tunnel.

sections.title: NAT Traversal
sections.content:
A NAT device can sit between the mobile node and the home agent in any mode, and between the node and the VPN gateway in mode mc. In modes c and f the node and home agent should use Mobile IPv4 NAT traversal (RFC 3519). In mode mc the node and VPN gateway should use IPsec NAT traversal (RFC 3947 and RFC 3948).

The TIA is normally routable inside the enterprise, but it can come from a private address space tied to the VPN gateway. In that case Mobile IPv4 NAT traversal should be used as well as IPsec NAT traversal in mode mc.
sections.plainLanguage: Some home routers rewrite addresses on the way through. The memo says which existing tricks to use so the messages still find their way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The solution was designed with the strong security that enterprise connectivity needs in mind. Concerns about detecting a trusted network and then dropping the VPN tunnel are described in RFC 5265.

One cost is stated plainly. A Registration Request sent from an untrusted network outside the IPsec tunnel reveals the i-HA's address, the node's identity including its NAI and home address, and the Authenticator value in the authentication extensions. This may be a concern in some deployments. For MOBIKE and NAT traversal security issues, the RFC points to RFC 4555, RFC 3519 and RFC 3947.
sections.plainLanguage: Knocking on the office door without the tunnel tells strangers a few things about you. That is the price of checking whether you are at work.
